title: Scale analytics with Amazon Redshift multi-warehouse enhancements
key_points: Materialized views now work across data sharing: consumers can build MVs on shared data and refresh producer MVs, and MV creation and Kinesis streaming-MV refresh can use concurrency scaling.
ALTER DISTSTYLE and ALTER TABLE APPEND run on remote warehouses, and COPY, auto-copy and zero-ETL ingestion can burst onto concurrency scaling so loading stops competing with queries.
Two patterns: a bank with staging, gold, ETL and user warehouses, and a gaming company isolating consumers on Serverless with their own MVs over a producer.
services: Amazon Redshift, Redshift data sharing, Redshift materialized views, Redshift concurrency scaling, zero-ETL integrations, Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
decision: Scale one warehouse vs producer/consumer warehouses with consumer-side MVs for workload isolation
authors: Raza Hafeez, Milind Oke, Ravi Animi, Satesh Sonti

title: Optimize your Tableau integration with Amazon Redshift Serverless
key_points: Checklist for Tableau on Redshift Serverless across five areas: star-schema data model, IAM-based secure connections, dashboard and connection tuning, cost control and query/join optimisation.
Core advice is a hybrid of live queries and extracts, with extracts acting as a cost buffer that keeps repeated dashboard loads off RPUs, and heavy logic pushed down into the warehouse.
Adds usage limits and monitoring to catch runaway queries.
services: Amazon Redshift Serverless, Tableau
decision: Live connection vs extracts (vs hybrid) for BI dashboards on a pay-per-use warehouse
authors: Tableau (Salesforce) — Nidhi Nayak, Adiascar Cisneros, Bill Tarr, Nita Shah

title: Amazon Redshift delivers faster performance for BI dashboards and real-time analytics
key_points: Redshift compiles each new query to C++; most queries reuse cached code, but uncached short queries paid a visible compile delay. Now they start on pre-built components while the optimised code compiles in the background.
On by default for provisioned and Serverless at no cost; mainly helps dashboards and agent-style ad hoc queries.
AWS reports the median compile time for uncached query segments fell from 4.3 seconds to 170 ms, and claims better price-performance than other warehouses in its own TPC-DS-derived test.
services: Amazon Redshift, Amazon Redshift Serverless
decision: When first-run compile latency matters for dashboards, and whether caching or warm-up workarounds are still needed
authors: Stefan Gromoll, Venkat Govindaraju, Kiran Chinta, Ravi Animi

title: Multi-Region identity-based access to Amazon Redshift and S3 Tables
key_points: Users and groups are managed once in IAM Identity Center and replicated to other Regions, so Redshift in a second Region resolves the same workforce identity through trusted identity propagation.
Redshift reads S3 Tables under Lake Formation grants and runs COPY/UNLOAD under S3 Access Grants, both tied to that one identity and visible in CloudTrail.
Useful gotchas: a replicated customer-managed KMS key is required, Access Grants are per Region, and Lake Formation locations need a custom role rather than the service-linked one.
services: Amazon Redshift, Amazon S3 Tables, AWS IAM Identity Center, AWS Lake Formation, Amazon S3 Access Grants, AWS Glue Data Catalog
decision: Per-Region IAM roles vs central Identity Center with trusted identity propagation for multi-Region warehouse and lake access
authors: Maneesh Sharma, Sandeep Adwankar, Rohit Vashishtha, Srividya Parthasarathy

title: Implement multi-tenant search with Amazon OpenSearch Serverless next generation
key_points: With the next-generation OpenSearch Serverless, each tenant gets its own collection inside a scale-to-zero collection group, and one regional endpoint per account routes requests by collection.
Gives isolation per tenant without per-tenant connection handling; code samples and limits included.
services: Amazon OpenSearch Serverless
authors: Jon Handler

title: Autonomous troubleshooting for Medallion Architecture with AWS DevOps Agent and Apache Spark Troubleshooting Agent
key_points: A bronze-silver-gold pipeline of three Glue jobs (orchestrated by MWAA, gold written to Redshift) fails in the gold step because the silver job quietly produced bad values; logs alone do not show it.

An EventBridge rule on Glue job failure triggers a Lambda that calls the DevOps Agent webhook; the agent uses the Spark Troubleshooting MCP server to trace the cause upstream and posts root cause and fixes to Slack.
Shows how a generic ops agent is extended with Spark-aware tools for data pipelines.
services: AWS Glue, AWS DevOps Agent, Apache Spark Troubleshooting Agent, Amazon Redshift, Amazon MWAA, Amazon EventBridge, AWS Lambda, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway
decision: Failure alert only vs agent-led root-cause investigation across medallion layers for failed Glue jobs
attaches_to: aws-bytes: Redshift ETL failure alert (planned); Data Quality Check (done) follow-up
authors: Mohammad Sabeel, Ishan Gaur

title: Why tombola chose Graviton-powered RG instances for Amazon Redshift
key_points: tombola (part of Flutter) would not change production without evidence, so it ran identical RA3 and RG clusters built from code and replayed heavy ETL, BI and light app queries chosen from production logs.
Four scenarios of increasing realism: cold cache, warm cache, a 1-to-20 stream concurrency sweep, and a 30-minute mixed workload; plus a separate test on Iceberg tables in S3 Tables.

AWS reports that in the mixed run RG finished heavy ETL about 1.85x faster at the median and 46% more queries overall, and that replacing four ra3.4xlarge with three rg.4xlarge cuts infrastructure cost by 25%.
services: Amazon Redshift, Redshift RG instances, Amazon S3 Tables, Apache Iceberg, Amazon MWAA, dbt, Amazon ECS
decision: Stay on RA3 vs move to RG, decided by a like-for-like replay of the real workload
authors: tombola — Prabhu Pandian, Akshay Srinivasan, Sidhanth Muralidhar, Vlad Siniavin

title: Detecting fraud patterns across Snowflake and AWS using SageMaker Data Agent
key_points: SageMaker Data Agent in Unified Studio notebooks adds Snowflake SQL generation, materialized view management and charting from prompts.
Fraud demo: query Snowflake transactions, land them in S3 Tables, join with risk profiles on AWS, schedule a materialized view and chart the result.
services: Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, Amazon SageMaker Data Agent, Snowflake, Amazon S3 Tables
authors: Akash Gupta, Anagha Barve, Siddharth Gupta, Mukesh Sahay, Eason Ma

title: Automating IT support with AI: How Nexthink uses OpenSearch Service to power self-service issue resolution
key_points: Nexthink's IT-support agent retrieves knowledge articles and past fixes through OpenSearch vector search, with embeddings created by Bedrock at indexing time and tenant filtering at query time.
Infrastructure is managed as code with Terraform, and Nexthink contributed provider resources back to open source.
services: Amazon OpenSearch Service, Amazon Bedrock, Terraform
authors: Nexthink — Rafael Ribeiro, Moe Haidar, Hajer Bouafif, Luca Perrozzi

title: Introducing Private Networking for Amazon MQ for RabbitMQ
key_points: Amazon MQ for RabbitMQ brokers can now make outbound connections to private resources (LDAP servers, other brokers, self-hosted RabbitMQ) through VPC Lattice, RAM and PrivateLink.
Replaces workarounds such as exposing identity providers publicly or load balancers with IP allowlists for federation.
services: Amazon MQ, Amazon VPC Lattice, AWS PrivateLink, AWS RAM
authors: Jean-Sébastien Dominique, Ishita Chakraborty

title: Modernize Amazon Redshift: RA3 to RG Migration best practices
key_points: Compares three ways to move RA3 clusters to Graviton-based RG: elastic resize (recommended), classic resize, and snapshot-restore-resize, with a node mapping table (for example three rg.4xlarge per four ra3.4xlarge).
Spells out side effects: during resize zero-ETL tables resync and data sharing pauses briefly; after snapshot-restore, zero-ETL integrations, DMS endpoints and datashares must be recreated.
AWS reports RG is up to 2.2x faster for warehouse and 2.4x for lake workloads at 30% lower price per vCPU, with no Spectrum scan charge; the RG lake engine is tuned mainly for Iceberg and Parquet.
services: Amazon Redshift, Redshift RG instances, AWS DMS, zero-ETL integrations, Redshift data sharing
decision: Elastic resize vs classic resize vs snapshot-restore for moving RA3 clusters to RG
authors: Nita Shah, Ankit Sahu, Ricardo Serafim, Vinayaka Gangadhar

title: AI-assisted data development with Kiro and SageMaker Unified Studio
key_points: Kiro, VS Code or Cursor connect over an SSH tunnel (via the AWS Toolkit) to a SageMaker Unified Studio Space, keeping the project's compute, permissions and governed data.
The Space auto-generates steering files so the coding agent knows the project setup from the first prompt.
services: Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, Kiro, AWS Toolkit for VS Code
authors: Zach Mitchell, Anchit Gupta, Leah Wagner, Majisha Namath Parambath, Bhargava Varadharajan

title: Access Amazon S3 data files directly using AWS Lake Formation permissions
key_points: Lake Formation can now vend temporary credentials for the S3 files behind a table it governs, so Spark code that reads paths directly (spark.read.parquet) is covered by the same grants as table queries.
Removes the parallel bucket policies or IAM policies kept for file-level access, and the drift between the two permission systems.
Demo: an EMR Spark job reads and writes the registered location while an analyst role queries the table in Athena.
services: AWS Lake Formation, Amazon S3, Amazon EMR, AWS Glue Data Catalog, Amazon Athena
decision: Separate bucket/IAM policies vs Lake Formation-vended credentials for file-level access to governed tables
authors: Aarthi Srinivasan, Archana Inapudi, Anandkumar Kaliaperumal, Mitali Sheth, Srinivasan Krishnasamy

title: Building AI shopping agent using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime and Amazon OpenSearch Service
key_points: A shopping assistant built with Strands Agents on AgentCore Runtime retrieves products from an OpenSearch index enriched with embeddings through ML connectors and an ingest pipeline.
Step-by-step setup of the index, the agent and its access to OpenSearch.
services: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Amazon OpenSearch Service, Strands Agents, Amazon Bedrock
authors: Omama Khurshid, Canberk Keles, Jumana Nagaria

title: Real-time CDC from Aurora PostgreSQL to Amazon S3 Tables using Debezium and Firehose
key_points: Debezium on MSK Connect reads Aurora PostgreSQL's logical replication and sends changes from all tables into one Kafka topic; Firehose pulls from MSK, a Lambda flattens each event, and Firehose applies inserts, updates and deletes to Iceberg tables in S3 Tables.
The target tables hold the current state of the source, not an append-only change log; one Firehose stream serves many tables via per-record routing metadata.
Deployed with CDK; queried from Athena with Lake Formation controlling access.
services: Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL, Debezium, Amazon MSK Connect, Amazon MSK, AWS Lambda, Amazon Data Firehose, Amazon S3 Tables, Apache Iceberg, Amazon Athena, AWS Lake Formation
decision: DMS vs zero-ETL vs Debezium + Firehose for Aurora PostgreSQL CDC into current-state Iceberg tables
attaches_to: aws-bytes: change data capture - DMS vs zero-ETL (later)
authors: Chintan Agrawal

title: Choosing the right workflow orchestration service for your use case: Amazon MWAA and AWS Step Functions
key_points: Frames the choice by workflow traits: stateful vs independent steps, run length, built-in scheduling, restart from a failed step, integration breadth and per-step permissions.
MWAA fits long, interdependent batch pipelines with schedules and partial reruns; Step Functions fits event-driven, short serverless flows with retries, parallel branches and human approval.
Includes a decision tree, says the two are often used together, and briefly points to Lambda Durable Functions as a code-first third option.
services: Amazon MWAA, AWS Step Functions, AWS Lambda, Apache Airflow
decision: MWAA vs Step Functions (vs Lambda Durable Functions) for orchestrating data and application workflows
authors: Rajkumar Raghuwanshi, Nishad Mankar, Shuvajit Ghosh

title: Upgrade PySpark from Spark 3.5 to Spark 4.0 with AWS Spark Upgrade Agent
key_points: Part 2 of a series: the Spark Upgrade Agent (an MCP server driven from Kiro CLI) upgrades a PySpark app from EMR Serverless 7.0 to 8.0, rerunning the job and reading CloudWatch errors until it passes.
The four breaking changes it hits are typical: a removed legacy Parquet config, a renamed codec, and stricter character-encoding rules.
A data comparison against the old version flags a mismatch that turns out to be previously garbled text now correct, a reminder to trace every difference to a code change.
services: Amazon EMR Serverless, AWS Spark Upgrade Agent, Apache Spark, Kiro, Amazon CloudWatch
decision: Manual vs agent-driven Spark 3-to-4 upgrades, validated by output comparison
authors: Prasad Nadig, Bezuayehu Wate, Chuhan Liu, Keerthi Chadalavada, Pradeep Patel, Karthik Prabhakar

title: Build stateful streaming applications with Apache Spark 4.0 on Amazon EMR Serverless
key_points: Spark 4.0's transformWithState API adds timers, state expiry, schema evolution and multiple state variables to Structured Streaming.
Example: IoT devices send heartbeats into Kinesis, a Spark job on EMR Serverless keeps per-device state and fires a timer to alert through SNS when a device goes silent, then notices recovery.
Covers job setup, IAM and a CLI-driven test of offline and recovery cases.
services: Amazon EMR Serverless, Apache Spark, Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, Amazon SNS
decision: Spark transformWithState vs Flink vs Lambda consumer for timer-based stateful detection on a stream
authors: Raj Ramasubbu, Praveen Krishnamoorthy Ravikumar, Rekha Veeraraghavan

title: Beyond JSON blobs: Implementing the VARIANT data type in Apache Iceberg V3
key_points: Iceberg V3's VARIANT type stores semi-structured JSON in a binary form with frequently used fields split into their own Parquet columns, so queries read only the fields they need instead of parsing whole strings.
Walkthrough creates a V3 table with a VARIANT column on EMR Serverless (Spark 4.0, Glue catalog) and extracts fields with variant_get().
Part 1 of a series; the benchmark against plain string storage comes in part 2. Natural counterpart to Redshift SUPER.
services: Apache Iceberg, Amazon EMR Serverless, Apache Spark, AWS Glue Data Catalog, Amazon S3
decision: JSON as string vs shredded columns vs VARIANT (lake) vs SUPER (warehouse) for evolving semi-structured payloads
authors: Arun Shanmugam, Ron Ortloff, Suthan Phillips, Xiaoxuan Li

title: Announcing general availability of Apache Spark 4.0 on Amazon EMR
key_points: Spark 4.0 is GA on EMR Serverless, EMR on EC2 and EMR on EKS via the new emr-spark-8.0 release, which also trims the bundled components to patch.
Headline features: Spark Connect, the VARIANT type and Iceberg V3, SQL scripting, Python data source API and UDF changes, and queryable streaming state.
AWS reports the EMR runtime runs Spark up to 4.5x faster than open-source Spark; includes migration and compatibility notes.
services: Amazon EMR, Amazon EMR Serverless, Apache Spark, Apache Iceberg
decision: Stay on Spark 3.5 vs move to Spark 4.0 (emr-spark-8.0) and when
authors: Suthan Phillips, Al MS, Kiki Nwangwu, Karthik Prabhakar

title: Announcing Spark Connect on Amazon EMR Serverless: Interactive PySpark development, anywhere
key_points: Spark Connect now works on EMR Serverless (release 7.13+): a local IDE or notebook keeps its Python session while Spark work runs remotely, ending the package-deploy-check loop.
Each session is its own AWS resource, so IAM permissions, cost tags, CloudTrail audit and config overrides apply per session, with a Spark UI and session history.
Third Spark Connect launch after EMR on EC2 and EKS; the serverless one is closest to how Glue is used.
services: Amazon EMR Serverless, Apache Spark, Spark Connect
decision: Package-and-submit vs interactive Spark Connect sessions for developing Spark jobs against real data
authors: Al MS, Melody Yang, Kiki Nwangwu

title: Unlock cost savings with incremental snapshot billing for Amazon Redshift Serverless and Amazon Redshift RG
key_points: From June 2026, manual snapshots on Redshift Serverless and RG are billed only for data blocks that are unique across all snapshots in the account; RA3 keeps the old model and existing snapshots switch over automatically.
Makes frequent snapshots, long compliance retention and cross-Region DR copies cheap, and closes the gap left by Serverless's 24-hour free recovery points.
AWS reports that a 10 TB workgroup changing 5% a day with seven daily snapshots pays for about 13 TB of unique snapshot data instead of seven full copies.
services: Amazon Redshift, Amazon Redshift Serverless, Redshift RG instances
decision: Snapshot frequency and retention on Serverless/RG now that only changed blocks are billed, vs keeping RA3
authors: Nidhi Nayak, Amy Huang, Raza Hafeez, Sushmita Barthakur

title: Migrate JMS applications to Amazon MQ for RabbitMQ with minimal changes
key_points: Amazon MQ for RabbitMQ 4+ ships the RabbitMQ JMS client support, so Java JMS apps move off ActiveMQ or on-premises brokers by changing the connection factory and endpoint only.
Includes an ActiveMQ-to-RabbitMQ example with validation and CloudWatch monitoring; non-Java services can then consume the same messages over AMQP.
services: Amazon MQ, RabbitMQ, Amazon CloudWatch
authors: Vinodh Kannan Sadayamuthu, Akhil Melakunta, Vignesh Selvam

title: Query Amazon Redshift using natural language with Kiro
key_points: Connects the Kiro coding agent to the Redshift MCP server so clusters, schemas and tables are discovered and queried in plain English, including comparisons across clusters and schema documentation.
Queries through the MCP tool run read-only, but the agent also has a shell, so write-capable IAM credentials bypass that guard; least-privilege IAM is the real control.
Stresses checking generated SQL, since wrong joins or filters can look plausible.
services: Amazon Redshift, Redshift MCP server, Kiro, Model Context Protocol (MCP)
decision: Console query editor vs MCP-connected coding agent for ad hoc warehouse questions, and how tightly to scope its IAM
attaches_to: dbt-pipelines (Redshift Serverless); aws-bytes: GenAI on data (later)
authors: Hitesh Dodiya

title: Build governance dashboards for Amazon SageMaker Catalog with AWS Quick
key_points: Follow-up to the catalog metadata export post: Quick Sight reads the exported metadata through Athena and charts undocumented assets, missing owners and stale metadata.
Visuals are built from natural-language prompts; mostly console steps.
services: Amazon SageMaker Catalog, Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, Amazon Quick Sight, Amazon Athena, Amazon S3 Tables
authors: Steve Phillips, Rohith Kayathi, Pradeep Misra, Ramesh H Singh

title: Accelerate SQL development with SageMaker Data Agent in Query Editor
key_points: SageMaker Data Agent inside the Unified Studio query editor turns plain-language questions into SQL for Athena or Redshift, reading real table metadata from the Glue catalog.
It keeps context across the session, proposes a step-by-step plan for multi-part questions that the user approves, and offers a one-click fix for failed queries.
Demo uses a public California schools dataset.
services: Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, Amazon SageMaker Data Agent, Amazon Athena, Amazon Redshift, AWS Glue Data Catalog
decision: Hand-written SQL vs catalog-aware agent with plan approval for exploratory analysis
authors: Jason Ramos, Jessica Cheng, Siddharth Gupta, Olena Mursalova, Sanjana Sekar

title: Schedule notebook runs in Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio
key_points: SageMaker Unified Studio notebooks can now run in the background, on a recurring schedule, and with parameters so one notebook serves several regions or segments.
Notebooks can be chained into workflows, and failed runs can be debugged with an AI assistant.
services: Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio
authors: Shivani Mehendarge, Regan Perk, Qazi Ashikin

title: Amazon OpenSearch Service: Mechanisms to secure your domain
key_points: Walks through OpenSearch Service's three security layers: network placement, the domain access policy, and fine-grained access control down to documents and fields.
Shows the settings for both a public domain and a VPC domain, plus encryption in transit and at rest.
services: Amazon OpenSearch Service
authors: Imtiaz Sayed, Narendra Gupta

title: Capture data lineage of Amazon EMR spark jobs into Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio
key_points: EMR 7.11+ has built-in OpenLineage support, so Spark jobs emit input/output and column-level lineage to SageMaker Catalog after a configuration change, with no code added to the jobs.
Demo: two Spark jobs join HR CSV files into Iceberg tables registered in the Glue catalog, and the resulting lineage graph is browsed in SageMaker Unified Studio.
Part of a wider set of OpenLineage integrations that also covers Glue, EMR Serverless and Redshift.
services: Amazon EMR, Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, Amazon SageMaker Catalog, OpenLineage, Apache Iceberg, AWS Glue Data Catalog
decision: Hand-documented lineage vs engine-emitted OpenLineage events into a central catalog for impact analysis and audits
authors: Jose Romero, Yanick Houngbedji
